title: Slim context bridge and loss-tolerant KV-windowing for SDK request instrumentation
creator: Anjali Rao
description: Problem: SDKs currently attach a relatively large, highly mutable propagation header that increases request latency, causes variability in header arrival across async boundaries, and occasionally corrupts the serving runtime's KV cache when partial headers are processed. This ticket introduces a slim context bridge implemented in the SDK (Node + Python) and a loss-tolerant KV-windowing strategy in the runtime to ensure safe, low-overhead propagation across sync/async boundaries and worker handoffs. Objectives: (1) reduce per-request propagation cost and header size variance, (2) make propagation resilient to partial header delivery and reordered segments, (3) preserve compatibility with legacy headers and rollout safely with feature flags.
acceptance_criteria: Node and Python SDKs add slim-bridge option behind feature flag and default to off for initial rollout
Measured median propagation overhead <200us on our benchmark (node-http, python-uvicorn) at 95th percentile QPS profile
Runtime KV-windowing rejects cache updates from incomplete/aged context segments and logs a traceable diagnostic when a segment is dropped
End-to-end tracing shows preserved parent-child relationships for >=99.5% of sampled requests during a 1h smoke run across internal staging services
Gradual rollout documented and automated in console feature flags with canary targeting by service and region
tasks: Design slim header format and segment framing (Anjali)
Implement slim-bridge encoder/decoder in python-sdk (Ivy Park)
Add feature flag plumbing to SDKs and runtime (infra)
Introduce KV-windowing guard in runtime kernel (runtime team)
Add unit + integration tests for header reassembly and aged-segment dropping
Benchmark propagation cost on standard harness and record baselines
Create console rollout plan and observability dashboards for early metrics
implementation_notes: Header format: base64 URL-safe compacted JSON with fixed 4-byte magic + varint segment index
Segments are reassembled by the SDK before sending; partial segments are allowed across queue handoffs but tagged with sequence stamps

KV-windowing: runtime stores per-request recent-segment-window (by request-id) and requires a full reassembly before applying cache writes; aged segments older than 5s are dropped with diagnostic metric increment
Fallback: if slim header absent, fall back to existing legacy propagation header to maximize compatibility
Sampling: keep existing sampling decision in a small fixed field so downstream collectors are not required to infer sampling from full header
test_plan: Unit tests for encoder/decoder edges: corrupted segments, out-of-order assembly, duplicate segments
Integration test: Node SDK -> edge proxy -> runtime; simulate WebSocket and worker-queue handoffs where segments arrive delayed
Chaos test: randomly drop segments (10%, 30%) and ensure no KV corruption and acceptable partial-trace loss rates
Performance test: run 30m bench across node-http and python-uvicorn harness to measure median and 95th latency impact
Consumer acceptance: QA team to run staging canary for 24h and sign off if trace fidelity >99% and overhead <200us
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Merge behind feature flag disabled by default (code review + automated CI)
Phase 1 canary: Enable for 5% of internal staging traffic for 24h -> monitor trace_coverage, header_drop_rate, propagation_latency
Phase 2 expanded canary: 20% traffic, add runtime KV-windowing in canary pool, monitor for 48h
Phase 3: Gradual 100% enable with daily roll increments and automated rollback on threshold breach
Emergency rollback: disable feature flag in SDK and runtime, or flip sampling to legacy header-only mode
risks: Incorrect reassembly could lead to dropped trace continuity — mitigated by unit/integration tests and conservative defaults
Edge cases for long-lived connections (websockets/streaming) may produce many small segments; we will bound segment rate and use sticky session heuristics
KV-windowing logic could add memory overhead for high fanout requests; we will limit window life to 5s and cap per-request buffer size
Backward compatibility: older runtime versions must not crash when receiving new slim header — ensure runtime ignores unknown header shapes when feature flag off
observability_steps: Create dashboard: OBS / Propagation - latency & fidelity (time series + heatmap)
Add alerts: header_drop_rate > 0.5% sustained for 10m, propagation_latency_p95 > 5000us
Add debug view: sample raw headers for failed reassemblies with anonymized IDs

notes: This ticket intentionally focuses on SDK-side encoding/decoding and a conservative runtime guard rather than attempting to change runtime cache semantics globally. The goal is minimal blast radius with measurable latency improvements and safer KV writes across asynchronous boundaries.
